chief_complaint: decreased urine output and elevated creatinine after diarrhea
hpi_details: A 20-year-old female presents to the clinic with 3 days of profuse watery diarrhea followed by a marked decrease in urine output over the last 24 hours. She reports generalized fatigue and lightheadedness on standing but denies fever, blood in stool, or NSAID use.
ideas: She thinks she contracted severe food poisoning that left her so dehydrated that her body has no fluid left to produce urine.
concerns: She is worried that her kidneys have suffered permanent damage and that she will collapse during her university final exams this week.
expectations: She hopes to receive an IV fluid drip to rehydrate quickly and medicine to stop the diarrhea so she can return home today.

investigation_events.title: Urgent kidney function assessment
investigation_events.availability_message: Urgent kidney function and renal index results are now available. Isotonic fluid replacement should proceed based on the clinical volume depletion.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Kidney Injury (prerenal) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Kidney Injury (prerenal) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management includes IV hydration to restore renal perfusion and holding nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, ACEi), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: decreased urine output and elevated creatinine after diarrhea

Key HPI features: A 20-year-old female presents to the clinic with 3 days of profuse watery diarrhea followed by a marked decrease in urine output over the last 24 hours. She reports generalized fatigue and lightheadedness on standing but denies fever, blood in stool, or NSAID use.
Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: BP 96/60, HR 104, orthostatic. Dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor. Labs: BUN 42 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.8 mg/dL (baseline 0.8), BUN:Cr ratio >20:1, FeNa <1%.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Kidney Injury (prerenal).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute tubular necrosis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Confusion or very low blood pressure.
management_principles: Initiate IV hydration (isotonic saline) to restore renal perfusion, and hold nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors)
Consult nephrology if creatinine fails to improve or urine output remains low despite adequate hydration
Counsel patient on maintaining oral hydration and recognizing red-flag symptoms warranting return
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for Kidney Disease

reference_soap.subjective: 20F presents with 3 days of profuse watery diarrhea followed by a marked decrease in urine output over the last 24 hours, with associated fatigue and lightheadedness on standing. Denies fever, blood in stool, or NSAID use. Labs today reveal an elevated creatinine.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: BP 96/60, HR 104, orthostatic. Dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor. Labs: BUN 42 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.8 mg/dL (baseline 0.8), BUN:Cr ratio >20:1, FeNa <1%.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute kidney injury, prerenal in etiology, secondary to volume depletion from diarrhea.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Initiate IV hydration (isotonic saline) to restore renal perfusion. 2. Recheck BUN/creatinine after rehydration to confirm improvement. 3. Consult nephrology if creatinine fails to improve or urine output remains low despite adequate hydration. 4. Counsel patient on oral hydration and red-flag symptoms warranting return.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Acute Kidney Injury
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Acute Kidney Injury
Implement evidence-based management plan: IV hydration, hold nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, ACEi)

teaching.one_liner: Volume depletion from diarrhea reduces blood flow to the kidneys, causing a rise in creatinine that typically reverses with rehydration.
red_flags: Confusion or very low blood pressure

must_ask.say: Tell me about the diarrhea — how much and how long?
Have you been able to drink and keep fluids down?
Are you taking blood pressure medications or NSAIDs?
Do you feel dizzy when standing?

exam.finding: Young female appearing fatigued and dehydrated, alert and oriented.
Blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, heart rate 104 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Supine blood pressure 96/60 mmHg and pulse 104 beats/min; standing blood pressure drops to 82/52 mmHg and pulse increases to 124 beats/min with lightheadedness.
Dry oral mucous membranes and cracked lips, without pharyngeal erythema or exudate.
Flat neck veins with no jugular venous distension seen even when reclined.
Tachycardic with regular rhythm; normal S1 and S2 with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with no crackles, wheezes, or decreased breath sounds.
Soft and non-tender throughout; no suprapubic fullness, palpable bladder, or masses.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on either side.
Decreased skin turgor with delayed recoil; no rashes, petechiae, or purpura.
No peripheral edema in either lower extremity.
No joint swelling, warmth, erythema, or tenderness.
